readerTitle: A cheaper rival just opened. Do you cut your price?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (가정·사무실 청소 회사) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 싼 경쟁자는 사업 전체를 공격하지 않는다. 가격에 가장 민감한 고객만 떼어 간다. 그래서 대응은 가격표가 아니라 '누구를 지킬 것인가'에서 시작한다.
misconception: 더 싼 경쟁자가 나타나면 가격을 맞추거나 더 내려야 고객을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1980). Competitive Strategy. Free Press. (원가 우위, 차별화, 집중 전략과 '어중간한 위치' 개념)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 시간당 $40의 30% 할인 = $40 × 0.7 = $28. 가격 인하안 $30은 기존보다 시간당 $10 낮음.
결과 카드(6번)의 '대부분의 정기 고객 유지, 매출 일시 감소 후 안정'은 가상 시나리오의 전개일 뿐 일반적 통계가 아님. 문구에 'In this story'로 표시함.

cards.title: A cheaper rival just opened. Do you cut your price?
body: Marta runs a cleaning company with 14 employed cleaners. She serves homes and small offices at $40 an hour.
One Monday, a new booking app launches in her city. Its cleaners are freelancers, and its price is $28 an hour. You're Marta. Four decisions follow.

image.label: Two price tags on a cleaning bucket: $40 and $28
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청소 양동이 두 개가 나란히 있고 하나에는 "$40/hr", 다른 하나에는 "$28/hr" 가격표. $28 쪽에 스마트폰 화면이 살짝 보임. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Eight customers cancel in the first month.
body: Most of your customers are still booked. But eight have cancelled, and a few mentioned the app. What's your first move?

options.text: Drop your rate to $30 an hour to stop the bleeding
options.feedback: You lose $10 an hour on every customer, including the many who weren't leaving. And the app can go lower still, which starts a price war you're built to lose.

options.text: Call those who left and those who stayed, and find out who is leaving and why
options.feedback: It costs a few days. In return you learn whether the rival threatens your whole business or only one part of it.

options.text: Run ads about your quality and trained staff
options.feedback: The message may be right. But you don't know yet which customers need to hear it, so the money may land in the wrong place.

cards.title: Say you made the calls. A pattern appears.
body: Nearly everyone who left booked one-off deep cleans and compared prices online. Regular home clients and offices stayed. They mention the same cleaner every week, trusting someone with their keys, and problems fixed fast.

options.text: Launch a cheap $28 "basic" line to win back one-off jobs, and keep the regular service
options.feedback: You'd run two cost structures at once and blur what you stand for. The app is built for $28. You aren't, so you risk being average at both.

options.text: Focus on regular homes and offices, and let price-shopping one-off jobs go
options.feedback: You give up some revenue but put every hour into customers who value what you do best. The rival can have the segment it was built for.

options.text: Serve only offices from now on
options.feedback: A sharp focus, but it throws away regular home clients who also pay for trust and consistency. Narrow, but narrower than the evidence suggests.

cards.title: Say you chose to focus. Now, where do you invest?
body: The app will try to look just like you. You have a small budget to strengthen your position with regular clients. What do you spend it on?

options.text: Same team per client on a fixed schedule, extra training, and a short report after each visit
options.feedback: This builds on employed, stable staff. A platform with rotating freelancers would have to change its whole model to copy it.
Some clients will like it. But the app could add the same products next week, so the edge won't last.

options.text: Give regular clients a 10% loyalty discount
options.feedback: It hands margin to customers who told you they weren't leaving. It also tells them price is what you compete on.

cards.title: Your biggest office client gets a lower bid.
body: The office pays you $3,000 a month. The app's business arm bids $2,250, which is 25% less. The office manager says: "Match it, or we switch."

options.feedback: You keep the client but lose $9,000 a year. Other office clients will hear about it and ask for the same.

options.text: Hold your price, show what they'd lose, and offer to lock today's rate for two years in return for a longer contract
options.feedback: You protect your price and make your difference visible: vetted staff with keys, the same team, fixes within a day. The small concession buys commitment, not a lower rate.

options.text: Let them go without a meeting
options.feedback: Your price stays intact, but you skip the conversation. The manager may not know what the cheaper bid leaves out.

cards.title: A cheaper rival splits your customers in two.
body: In this story, Marta loses most one-off jobs and keeps most regular clients. Revenue dips, then steadies at a healthier price.
The lesson behind it: a low-price rival rarely attacks everyone. It pulls away the customers for whom **price matters most**. Those were never the customers your advantage was built on.
So the response is not one price. Match only where low cost is your strength. Everywhere else, strengthen the reason people pay more.

image.label: Customers split into two groups: price-driven and loyal
image.brief: 고객 아이콘 무리가 가운데 선을 기준으로 둘로 갈라짐. 왼쪽 작은 무리는 "$28" 표지판 쪽으로, 오른쪽 큰 무리는 "Same team, trusted, fixed fast" 표지판 쪽으로 이동. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Holding your price only works if your difference is real.
body: Test it honestly. Did customers name your advantage on their own, or only after you prompted them? If the rival is cheaper and just as good, the group you keep will keep shrinking. Then you need lower costs or a new position.
Focus also has a cost. A smaller customer base must still cover your fixed costs, like vans, insurance and office rent.
cards.softwareNote: When a cheaper tool launches, accounts that use only basic features usually leave first. Check churn by plan and usage before cutting price. The answer is often to deepen what heavy users rely on, such as integrations and support.

cards.title: Answer a cheaper rival with focus, not a price cut.
body: Each decision used an idea from this unit:
list: **Ask before cutting:** you weren't the cost leader, so a price war played to the rival's strength
**Pick a segment:** focus, and avoid being stuck in the middle with a cheap line
**Invest in the hard-to-copy:** stable teams a freelance model can't easily match
**Hold the price:** a sustainable advantage is one customers still pay for under pressure
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list your last five lost customers. Next to each, write whether they left for price or for something else.
